subtype: Approach: avoiding the topic to stay hopeful [Pitfall]
passage:
I live next door to Dilnaz's family, so I saw what happened, and I still don't know what each person was really feeling. When Dilnaz's father got the news, the family made a rule: no one says the word. "It will pass," Dilnaz's mother told visitors. Whenever I asked how things were, Dilnaz smiled and changed the subject to the weather.
For months nobody sat down to ask what he wanted from his care, or how bills would be handled. Papers sat in a drawer.
Then one night the ambulance came. In the hospital corridor I watched the family sign forms in a rush, with no clue about his wishes. Dilnaz stood by the wall, very quiet.
— Nitin

qa.q: What was the rule the family made when the news came?
qa.a: The rule was that no one says the word.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have been feeling when smiling and changing the subject?
qa.a: Dilnaz may have been frightened and holding on to hope, though Nitin cannot be sure, since the smile and quick change of subject could be protection.

qa.q: What could the family have done during the months before the emergency?
qa.a: They could have set aside a calm hour to ask the father what he wanted and to look at the papers together.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin to watch the family in the corridor?
qa.a: Nitin felt helpless and sorry, watching people who cared deeply sign forms without knowing the father's wishes.

grounding: The account shows a family refusing to discuss how serious a diagnosis is, delaying talks on care and money until an emergency forces rushed decisions.

January. After Appachan's diagnosis, Jomon tries to raise it at dinner. "Should we talk about what he'd want if things get worse?" His mother puts down her spoon. "Don't bring bad luck into this house." His sister Ritu changes the subject to her exams.
April. Appachan seems stronger. Nobody asks where his bank papers are, or whether he would want to be treated at home or in hospital. Jomon writes a list of questions and keeps it in his drawer.
July. At 2 am Appachan collapses. In the emergency ward the doctor asks, "Has he said anything about intensive treatment? Who signs?" Jomon's mother is crying; Ritu is on the phone with relatives. Nobody knows. Jomon signs forms he barely reads. Later, looking for the insurance card, they find the bank papers are in a locker whose key no one can find.

qa.q: What did Jomon's mother say at dinner in January?
qa.a: "Don't bring bad luck into this house."

qa.q: How did Jomon feel keeping the list of questions in his drawer?
qa.a: Jomon was probably anxious and frustrated, wanting to plan but afraid of upsetting the family again.

qa.q: What could the family have done in April, when Appachan seemed stronger?
qa.a: Gently asked Appachan about his wishes and where his papers were, perhaps with the doctor's help, while things were calm.

qa.q: How does Ritu experience the family's avoidance?
qa.a: Ritu changes the subject in January and is on the phone in a crisis in July, likely frightened and unprepared.

grounding: It shows a family refusing to talk about a serious diagnosis to stay hopeful, so talks about care wishes and finances wait until an emergency forces rushed decisions.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the topic to stay hopeful [Pitfall]
passage:
Anjali Bua looked at Ojas over her glasses when he said the family shouldn't talk about Nani's illness, to keep her spirits up. "Let me tell you about my father, beta. When I was twenty-five, the doctors told us his illness was serious. And we decided, all of us, not to talk about it. My mother said it would make him lose hope. So we smiled and spoke about weddings and cricket.
Nobody asked him whether he wanted to be in hospital or at home at the end. Nobody asked where his papers were, or what he wanted done with the shop. We thought we had time.
Then one night he couldn't breathe. At the hospital, strangers asked us questions only he could have answered. We made choices in ten minutes in a corridor. I still don't know if they were the ones he would have made.
Hope is good, Ojas. But ask Nani what she wants while she can tell you."

qa.q: What did the family talk about instead of the illness?
How does Anjali feel about the choices made in the corridor?
qa.a: She still feels uncertain and regretful, not knowing if they were what her father would have wanted.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have changed the ending, and why?
qa.a: Asking her father about his wishes and papers while he could answer, so the family wasn't deciding for him in ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Anjali's father have felt being kept in cheerful talk?
qa.a: He may have felt protected but also unheard, never asked what he himself wanted.

grounding: It shows a young woman's family avoiding talk of her father's serious illness to stay hopeful, so wishes about care and affairs are never discussed until an emergency.
